issues.legal_issue: Property purchased in a woman's name with money provided by her husband is not thereby a gift of that property for purposes of classifying her property on succession.
material_facts: The conveyance for the principal property was made in the mother's name.
The father provided the entire consideration for the purchase.
The appellant claimed the property passed exclusively to her as a gift to her mother, while her brothers were also heirs if it was property acquired by purchase.
issues.conclusion: The property was acquired by purchase and did not fall within the category of property gifted to the mother; the source of the purchase money did not change that classification.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 10(2)(b) and 10(2)(d) of the Mysore Hindu Law Women's Rights Act, 1933, section 10(2)(b) covers a gift of the very property in specie, whereas property acquired by purchase falls under section 10(2)(d), regardless of the source of the funds used. A gift of money followed by purchase of another property does not make the purchased property itself a gift. The court also referred to the requirement that a gift of immovable property worth more than Rs. 100 be made by registered deed.

predicates.succession_recovery_suit: A claimant brings a suit seeking property said to have devolved from a deceased woman.
predicates.purchase_deed_names_woman: The conveyance for the property names the woman as purchaser.
predicates.husband_provided_purchase_money: The woman's husband provided the money used to pay the purchase consideration.

issues.definition: When a succession recovery suit concerns property conveyed to a woman using money provided by her husband, the property remains classified as purchased property rather than as property gifted to her.

issues.legal_issue: A husband's payment of the purchase consideration does not defeat the title of the wife named in the conveyance when his conduct acknowledges her ownership.
material_facts: The sale deed conveyed the principal property to the mother.
The father provided the entire purchase consideration and managed the property.
Letters from the father and mother treated the property as belonging to the mother, including the father's statements about her estate and her making a will concerning it.
issues.conclusion: The property belonged to the mother, and the High Court erred in finding that it belonged to the father and had been conveyed to the mother benami.
issues.legal_principle: The court considered the conveyance and the father's admissions in correspondence as evidence of the mother's title. It held that management and possession by the husband were consistent with his managing property on his wife's behalf and did not, by themselves, undermine her title.

rule.if: property_title_dispute and conveyance_names_wife and husband_paid_purchase_price and husband_acknowledged_wifes_ownership

predicates.property_title_dispute: A dispute arises over whether property conveyed to a wife belonged to her or to her husband.
predicates.conveyance_names_wife: The conveyance for the property names the wife as its recipient.
predicates.husband_paid_purchase_price: The husband paid the consideration for the property.
predicates.husband_acknowledged_wifes_ownership: The husband made statements or acted in ways acknowledging that the property belonged to his wife.

issues.definition: When a title dispute involves a conveyance to a wife, payment by her husband, and his acknowledgment of her ownership, the wife held title to the property.

issues.legal_issue: A suit seeking relief concerning an estate shared by co-heirs is incompetent when a necessary co-heir is not joined.
material_facts: The mother died intestate, and the appellant and her two brothers were heirs to the property under the applicable succession rule.
The appellant pursued the suit on the basis that she alone was entitled to the property and did not join her brothers.
The respondents raised non-joinder in the trial court, and the appellant's suit sought recovery of the property.
issues.conclusion: The brothers were necessary parties, the estate could be represented only with all three heirs before the court, and the suit was incompetent for non-joinder.
issues.legal_principle: Order I Rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure does not save a suit where necessary parties have not been joined. Under Order I Rule 10(2), a court may direct that necessary parties be joined, but the judgment states that this should be done at the trial stage and without prejudice to those parties' plea of limitation. A suit by one of several co-heirs for relief concerning the estate takes the character of a suit for partition, and the estate is represented only when all heirs are before the court. The court followed Naba Kumar Hazra v. Radheshyam Mahish, A.I.R. 1931 P.C. 229.

rule.if: estate_recovery_suit and multiple_coheirs_share_estate and claimant_seeks_relief_as_sole_heir and coheir_not_joined

predicates.estate_recovery_suit: A claimant brings a suit seeking relief concerning property left by a deceased person.
predicates.multiple_coheirs_share_estate: More than one heir is entitled to succeed to the estate.
predicates.claimant_seeks_relief_as_sole_heir: The claimant pursues the suit on the basis that the claimant alone is entitled to the property.
predicates.coheir_not_joined: An heir who shares entitlement to the estate is not made a party to the suit.

issues.definition: When a claimant seeks estate-related relief as the sole heir despite other heirs sharing the estate, omitting a co-heir makes the suit incompetent for non-joinder.

issues.legal_issue: A claimant who persists in proceeding without necessary co-heirs cannot add them at a late stage after having had earlier opportunities to do so.
material_facts: The respondents expressly raised non-joinder in the trial court, and a specific issue was framed on that point.
The appellant did not seek to add her brothers during the trial or before the High Court.
The appellant sought to add them only after the appeal had been heard and stood over for possible settlement.
issues.conclusion: The application to add the brothers as parties was rejected as too late.
issues.legal_principle: Although Order I Rule 10(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure permits the addition of necessary parties, the court held that the defect should have been addressed at the trial stage. It applied Naba Kumar Hazra v. Radheshyam Mahish, A.I.R. 1931 P.C. 229, which rejected an attempt to add necessary parties on appeal where the defect had been raised from the outset and there had been ample opportunity to remedy it.

rule.if: civil_appeal and nonjoinder_raised_early and claimant_had_opportunity_to_add_party and claimant_persisted_without_party and addition_sought_at_late_stage

predicates.civil_appeal: The matter is an appeal in a civil suit.
predicates.nonjoinder_raised_early: The opposing party raised the absence of a necessary party at an early stage of the proceedings.
predicates.claimant_had_opportunity_to_add_party: The claimant had an earlier opportunity to seek the addition of the omitted party.
predicates.claimant_persisted_without_party: The claimant continued the proceedings without adding the omitted party.
predicates.addition_sought_at_late_stage: The claimant first sought to add the necessary party at a late stage of the proceedings.

issues.definition: In a civil appeal, a late request to add a necessary party is rejected when non-joinder was raised early, the claimant had an earlier opportunity to remedy it, and the claimant persisted without doing so.
